commons.title: Dzamadan - Gorani Men`s costume is richly decorated with a vest.jpg
commons.description: Gorani folk costume belongs to the general Balkan type, it is partially preserved and used in everyday use. The materials from which parts of Men`s wear are made are different and change over time. Previously, wool and cotton were used exclusively, while silk and synthetic materials were increasingly used in recent times.
commons.editorial_reason: Title and description explicitly identify Gorani men’s costume; the decorated vest is visibly traditional dress.

commons.title: Torlak dialects map en.png
commons.credit: The original uploader was Jingiby at English Wikipedia.; derivative work by Nikola Stojanoski
commons.description:
Map showing one representation of the geographic distribution of Torlak/Prizren–Timok varieties and neighbouring South Slavic dialect groups in parts of Serbia, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Bulgaria and Romania.
The genealogical classification of Torlak/Prizren–Timok and some of the boundaries shown on this map are disputed in linguistic literature. Živojinović (2021) notes that Torlak has been classified both as Štokavian/Serbian and as Bulgarian, and specifically states that the Gorani and Carashovan areas shown here are disputed and are not always considered Torlak. The same source reproduces this map as the closest available approximation, while noting that it does not represent the current distribution.
Sources and references:

Browne, Wayles (2003) "Serbo-Croat" in     The Slavonic Languages, Routledge, p. 383  ISBN:  9781136861376. 
Ivić, Pavle (1956)       Dijalektologija srpskohrvatskog jezika: uvod i štokavsko narečje, Novi Sad:  Matica srpska, p. 218  
Bulgarian Dialect Atlas (Български диалектен атлас), Bulgarian Academy of Sciences: vol. III, South-Western Bulgaria (1975), and vol. IV, North-Western Bulgaria (1981). The original upload description cited volumes III and IV but gave 1974 for both.
Živojinović, Jelena (2021) "Torlak clitic doubling: A cross-linguistic comparison" in     Advances in formal Slavic linguistics 2018, Berlin:  Language Science Press, pp. 423–441  DOI:  10.5281/zenodo.5483122. 
The underlying map was described by the original uploader as reworked by Пламен Цветков from a Bulgarian-language version.
commons.editorial_reason: The image is a dialect distribution map, not visible Gorani cultural material.
